stances.claim: Significantly, Japanese PM Shinzo Abe visited the Philippines right after the LDP's July 24 2013 electoral sweep of the upper house -- consolidating the LDP's earlier Dec 16 2012 landslide in the more powerful lower house and Abe's Dec 26 2012 election as PM by 328 of 480 lower-house members. This is a dazzling political grand slam by Abe, who six years ago embarrassingly resigned as PM after losing Diet confidence -- only the second leader in Japan's history (after Shigeru Yoshida in 1948) to come back for a second term.

In the past decade Japan had revolving-door leadership changes (1-year-average PM term), aggravated by lethargic economy (China overtook Japan as world's second-largest economy two years before). For Filipinos with fixed-term six-year presidencies, the revolving-door phenomenon could be catastrophic. However, like mature parliamentary democracies (Britain, Canada, Australia), Japan's competent civil servants (not tarnished by partisan politics) kept the country going despite political instability -- but the disadvantage is that civil servants cannot supply vision and direction, which only elected leaders can.

The LDP's landslide in both houses gives Abe a stable term, assuring fulfillment of his vision (revitalize economy/defense/international relations). Japanese politicians, unlike Filipino counterparts, do not flip-flop and change political colors at their whim. Abe's visit right after his stunning victory shows his keen interest in prioritizing and solidifying friendship and partnership with the PH -- Japan may yet be the PH's best ally, rivaling century-old US relations.

Prior to Abe's visit, per Ambassador Manuel M. Lopez, Japan was already the PH's top trading partner ($16.33B two-way trade in 2012), top ODA source, one of the largest sources of FDI and foreign tourists (412,474 in 2012). Japan is low-profile-representative in the Malaysia-chaired foreign-monitoring-group on the MILF peace agreement; it also actively supports the PH stance to resolve the WPS dispute peacefully through UNCLOS arbitration.

The visit boosted the already strong 'strategic partnership' with Abe's announced 'Four Initiatives': (1) foster vibrant economy + Metro Manila transportation-infrastructure + 10-billion-yen ($100M) standby-emergency-credit for disaster recovery; (2) maritime cooperation including 10 patrol vessels for the PH Coast Guard via yen loan; (3) strengthen Mindanao Peace Process assistance; (4) people-to-people exchange via relaxed visa rules + more regular flights -- with PH tourists to Japan finding an automatic 30% discount from yen-to-dollar + dollar-to-peso depreciation.

Armed with an equally robust popular mandate (May 2013 LP victory ensuring full Congress support, retaining Belmonte as Speaker and getting close ally Drilon elected as SP, plus unprecedented 76% SWS / 73% Pulse Asia performance ratings), PNoy has enormous political capital to respond firmly to Abe's initiatives. In Pampango 'abe' means close friend or bosom buddy; PNoy hails from that Tarlac part imbibing the language. In holding their summit right after their grand political sweeps, PNoy and Abe may yet turn out to be bosom buddies -- and the Philippines and Japan may yet become BFFs (best friends forever), all for the mutual benefit of both leaders and both nations.
